chapters.title: Chapter 4: Beyond Percentages: Control, Rights and Exits

lessons.title: Down Rounds and Anti-Dilution: The Founder's Side of the Deal

children.text: Two years after the Series B, TiffinBox's growth has slowed and the funding market has turned. The only Series C on the table is ₹20 crore at a ₹60 crore pre-money valuation, against a ₹200 crore post-money two years ago. Meera expects to be diluted. What she has not read recently is the anti-dilution clause in the Series B documents, which decides whether she ends this round at 20.73% or at 15.84%.

body.text: A down round dilutes everyone. Anti-dilution decides whether it dilutes everyone equally or whether the founders and the team absorb the investors' share of the loss as well.

markDefs.definition: A clause protecting earlier investors if new shares are later issued at a lower price, by reducing the price at which their preference shares convert, so they receive more ordinary shares on conversion.

children.text: Every priced round in India gives investors

. It does not stop the down round. It adjusts the conversion price of the earlier preference shares downwards, so the same investment converts into more shares. Those extra shares come from the pool of ownership held by everyone without protection, which means the founders, the team and the angels.

body.caption: Three flavours of anti-dilution, from harshest to fairest

cells: Full ratchet
The earlier investor's conversion price resets to the new, lower price, however few shares are issued
Brutal. The investor is made whole as if they had invested at the new price
Narrow-based weighted average
Conversion price adjusts partially, using a share count that excludes options and other instruments
Painful but proportionate
Broad-based weighted average
Conversion price adjusts partially, using the full fully diluted share count including options
The market standard and the one to negotiate for

body.caption: Weighted average: NCP is the new conversion price, OCP the old one, A the shares outstanding before the round, B the shares the new money would have bought at the old price, and C the shares actually issued

children.text: TiffinBox has 35,071 fully diluted shares. The Series B investor put in ₹40 crore at ₹57,029 per share for 7,014 shares. The Series C raises ₹20 crore at a ₹60 crore pre-money valuation, which prices the new shares at ₹60,00,00,000 ÷ 35,071 = ₹17,108 each, so the new investor receives about 11,690 shares. Now apply each type of protection to the Series B.

Full ratchet: the Series B conversion price simply becomes the new price of ₹17,108. Its ₹40 crore now converts into ₹40,00,00,000 ÷ ₹17,108 = 23,381 shares, up from 7,014. That is 16,367 extra shares created out of thin air, all of which dilute everyone without protection.

Broad-based weighted average: A is 35,071 shares, B is ₹20,00,00,000 ÷ ₹57,029 = 3,507 shares, and C is 11,690 shares. NCP = ₹57,029 × (35,071 + 3,507) ÷ (35,071 + 11,690) = ₹57,029 × 38,578 ÷ 46,761 = ₹47,049. The Series B's ₹40 crore converts into ₹40,00,00,000 ÷ ₹47,049 = 8,502 shares, which is 1,488 extra.

Narrow-based weighted average: the only change is that A counts just the preference shares as converted, which is 5,000 plus 7,014 plus 7,014 = 19,028, rather than the full 35,071. NCP = ₹57,029 × (19,028 + 3,507) ÷ (19,028 + 11,690) = ₹41,836, giving 9,561 shares, which is 2,547 extra. A smaller A produces a bigger adjustment, which is exactly why the definition of A is worth negotiating.

body.text: A full ratchet rewards an investor for a single low-priced share. Even a small bridge issued cheaply can reset an entire round's conversion price. If a term sheet offers a ratchet, ask for it to be limited: broad-based weighted average instead, or at minimum a ratchet that applies only to issues above a minimum size and falls away after a defined period.

In India the adjustment is usually implemented by changing the conversion ratio of the existing compulsorily convertible preference shares rather than issuing fresh shares to the protected investor. There is also a pricing constraint to plan for: a fresh valuation is needed to support the new, lower price, and where non-resident investors are involved, FEMA pricing rules restrict issuing shares below fair value. A down round therefore needs your valuer and your company secretary involved early, not at signing.

body.label: Pay to play
body.value: Protection for those who keep funding
body.context: A pay-to-play clause says an investor keeps its anti-dilution and preference rights only if it participates pro rata in the down round. It is one of the few clauses that helps founders in bad times, because it converts passive protected investors into ordinary shareholders. Ask for it before you need it.

body.title: The ratchet's cost in shares
body.prompt: The Series B invested ₹40 crore at ₹57,029 per share. Under a full ratchet, its conversion price resets to the Series C price of ₹17,108 per share. How many shares does the Series B now hold? Round to the nearest whole share.
body.explanation: ₹40,00,00,000 ÷ ₹17,108 = about 23,381 shares, up from 7,014. The investor gains 16,367 shares without investing another rupee, and every one of those shares dilutes the founders, the team and the unprotected angels.

body.title: Name the harshest term
body.textWithBlank: Anti-dilution that resets an earlier investor's conversion price all the way down to the new issue price, however few shares are issued, is called a full ___.
body.explanation: A full ratchet makes the earlier investor whole as though they had invested at the new price. Weighted average formulas adjust only partially, in proportion to how many shares were issued cheaply.

body.title: Which definition should you fight for?
body.question: Your term sheet offers weighted average anti-dilution. Which definition of A, the pre-round share count in the formula, is best for founders?
options: Narrow-based, counting only preference shares as converted
Broad-based, counting all fully diluted shares including the option pool and convertibles
It makes no difference, because the formula is the same
Whichever produces the higher new conversion price for the investor's benefit
body.explanation: A larger A produces a smaller adjustment. At TiffinBox, broad-based gave the Series B 8,502 shares while narrow-based gave 9,561, a difference of 1,059 shares taken from everyone unprotected. Always negotiate for the broadest possible definition.

body.title: Price or structure
body.scenario: Your Gurugram healthtech raised ₹60 crore at ₹240 crore post-money two years ago. You have nine months of runway. Two offers are on the table for ₹35 crore. Offer A: ₹105 crore pre-money, standard 1x non-participating preference, broad-based weighted average anti-dilution, pay-to-play applying to all existing investors. Offer B: ₹235 crore pre-money so the headline barely moves, but with a 2x participating preference for the new money and a full ratchet. You hold 24% fully diluted.
body.prompt: Which do you take, and what do you check before deciding?
body.modelAnswer:
Start with what each offer really is. Offer A is an honest down round: the price falls, everyone including you is diluted, and the weighted average adjustment for earlier investors is proportionate. Offer B keeps the headline and sells the difference out of your exit proceeds: ₹35 crore at 2x participating means ₹70 crore comes off the top of any exit before anyone else is paid, and the new investor then still shares the remainder.

What to check before deciding:
1. Model both at three exit prices. At a ₹200 crore exit, Offer B's ₹70 crore preference plus participation can leave founders with very little, while Offer A's simple structure leaves the remainder split by ownership.
2. Total the preference stack under each. Under B it is the old ₹60 crore plus ₹70 crore, which is ₹130 crore that your exit must clear before ordinary shares see a rupee.
3. Look at the ratchet in B. Any future round below this price resets the new investor's conversion price completely, and the next round after a structured one is often lower.
4. Assess the pay-to-play in A. It pressures existing investors to keep funding you or lose their protections, which can be genuinely valuable when you raise again.
5. Ask what future investors will think. A 2x participating preference with a ratchet sits on the cap table until it is renegotiated, and many funds simply will not price a company carrying it.
6. Talk to your existing investors before choosing. Under A, their anti-dilution adjusts and they will have a view. Under B, their economics sit behind a large new preference.

The likely answer: take Offer A. The headline in B is a story told to people who will not be paying you, while the structure is a bill your own shareholders settle at exit. Use the nine months of runway to earn the next price rather than borrowing it from your own future proceeds.

body.title: Preparing for a possible down round
steps: Read the anti-dilution clause in every round you have closed, and note the type and the definition of the pre-round share count.
Model your stake under weighted average and under a full ratchet before you go out to raise.
Check whether any existing instrument would be triggered by a small bridge issued at a low price.
Add up the preference stack you would be creating under any structured alternative.
Ask for pay-to-play, so protections follow the investors who keep supporting the company.
Involve a registered valuer and your company secretary early, since a lower price needs support and non-resident pricing rules apply.
Consider a pool top-up for the team in the same round, because their options may be deep underwater.
Prefer an honest lower price over structure that keeps the headline and moves the cost to your exit.

cards.definition: A financing round priced below the price per share of the previous round.
A clause reducing an earlier investor's conversion price when shares are later issued more cheaply.
Anti-dilution that resets the earlier conversion price all the way to the new issue price.
A partial adjustment using the full fully diluted share count, the market standard and the most founder-friendly common form.
A partial adjustment using a smaller share count, usually only preference shares as converted, which produces a larger adjustment.
A clause under which an investor keeps its protections only by participating in later rounds.
A round that preserves the headline valuation by granting harsher economic terms such as multiples, participation or ratchets.

points: A down round is a lower price per share than the previous round, and it dilutes everyone.
Anti-dilution protects earlier investors by lowering their conversion price, and the extra shares come out of everyone unprotected.
Full ratchet resets the conversion price entirely. Weighted average adjusts it partially.
In TiffinBox's down round, founders end at 21.39% with no protection, 20.73% under broad-based weighted average, 20.28% under narrow-based and 15.84% under a full ratchet.
A larger pre-round share count in the formula means a smaller adjustment, so always negotiate the broad-based definition.
Pay-to-play is the clause that helps founders in bad times, because protections follow the investors who keep funding.
Structure that preserves a headline valuation is paid for out of your exit proceeds and can make the next round unfundable.
A down round needs a supporting valuation and, with non-resident investors, compliance with FEMA pricing rules.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods and the other companies and people described are fictional, and all prices, share counts and percentages are illustrative. The calculations apply anti-dilution to one round only and round share counts to whole shares, so real outcomes will differ where several rounds hold protection. Anti-dilution formulas, pricing requirements, valuation rules and FEMA conditions depend on your documents and change over time. Consult a qualified lawyer, registered valuer, company secretary or chartered accountant before pricing or closing any round.
